diplodocus:enwiki:7.title: Diplodocus (Second Dinosaur Rush and Diplodocus carnegii)

facts.statement: The first fossils of Diplodocus were discovered in 1877 by S. W. Williston.
facts.quote: The first fossils of Diplodocus were discovered in 1877 by S. W. Williston.

facts.statement: The genus name Diplodocus was coined by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878, referring to the double-beamed chevron bones on the tail underside.
facts.quote: The generic name, coined by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878, is a Neo-Latin term derived from Greek διπλός (diplos) "double" and δοκός (dokos) "beam", in reference to the double-beamed chevron bones located in the underside of the tail, which were then considered unique.

facts.statement: At least one specimen, AMNH FR 223, is potentially from the Tithonian stage, the youngest deposits of the formation.
facts.quote: although it may have made it into the Tithonian, with at least one specimen (AMNH FR 223) being potentially from among the youngest deposits of the formation.

facts.statement: Remains of Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus found in the same strata suggest they coexisted with Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Its great size may have been a deterrent to the predators Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus: their remains have been found in the same strata, which suggests that they coexisted with Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Modern mass estimates for D. carnegii range from 12 to 14.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: Modern mass estimates for D. carnegii have tended to be in the 12 - 14.8 MT range.

facts.statement: Diplodocus had small, forward-pointing, peg-like teeth located only in the front sections of the jaws.
facts.quote: Diplodocus had small, 'peg'-like teeth that pointed forward and were only present in the anterior sections of the jaws.

facts.statement: Diplodocus had a small braincase and a neck composed of at least 15 vertebrae.
facts.quote: Its braincase was small, and the neck was composed of at least 15 vertebrae.

facts.statement: When first described in 1991, David Gillette estimated D. hallorum to be 33 meters long.
facts.quote: When first described in 1991, discoverer David Gillette calculated it to be 33 m long based on isometric scaling with D. carnegii.

facts.statement: The estimated length of D. hallorum was revised downward to 29–33.5 meters after Gillette misplaced vertebrae 12–19 as vertebrae 20–27.
facts.quote: The estimated length was later revised downward to 30.5–35 m and later on to 29 - 33.5 m based on findings that show that Gillette had originally misplaced vertebrae 12–19 as vertebrae 20–27.

facts.statement: The middle part of the Diplodocus tail had oddly shaped chevron bones called "double beams," which gave the genus its name.
facts.quote: The middle part of the tail had "double beams" (oddly shaped chevron bones on the underside, which gave Diplodocus its name).

facts.statement: Diplodocus lacked claws on all front limb digits except one, which was unusually large, flattened, and detached from the hand bones.
facts.quote: Diplodocus lacked claws on all but one digit of the front limb, and this claw was unusually large relative to other sauropods, flattened from side to side, and detached from the bones of the hand.

facts.statement: Skin impressions discovered in 1990 showed that some diplodocids had narrow, pointed, keratinous spines similar to those on an iguana.
facts.quote: The discovery of partial diplodocid skin impressions in 1990 showed that some species had narrow, pointed, keratinous spines, much like those on an iguana.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the Diplodocus tail served a defensive, noisemaking, or tactile function.
facts.quote: Some speculation exists as to whether it may have had a defensive or noisemaking (by cracking it like a coachwhip) or, as more recently suggested, tactile function.

facts.statement: The type species of Diplodocus is D. longus, which is considered a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: type_species: Diplodocus longus (nomen dubium)

facts.statement: Subspecies include D. carnegii (Hatcher, 1901) and D. hallorum (Gillette, 1991), the latter originally classified as Seismosaurus.
facts.quote: subdivision: D. carnegii Hatcher, 1901 D. hallorum (Gillette, 1991) (originally Seismosaurus)

facts.statement: Seismosaurus is a synonym of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Seismosaurus Gillette, 1991

facts.statement: The first Diplodocus fossils were found in 1877 at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado, by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Wendell Williston.
facts.quote: The first record of Diplodocus comes from Marshall P. Felch's quarry at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado, when several fossils were collected by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Wendell Williston in 1877.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh named the first specimen Diplodocus longus in 1878.
facts.quote: The specimen was sent to the Yale Peabody Museum and was named Diplodocus longus ('long double-beam') by paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878.

facts.statement: Diplodocus was named during the Bone Wars, a competition between Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope.
facts.quote: Marsh named Diplodocus during the Bone Wars, his competition with Philadelphian paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope to collect and describe as many fossil taxa as possible.

facts.statement: The first complete diplodocid skull was collected in 1883 and consisted of an articulated skull, mandibles, and partial atlas.
facts.quote: One specimen (USNM V 2672), an articulated complete skull, mandibles, and partial atlas was collected in 1883, and was the first complete diplodocid skull to be reported.

facts.statement: In 1897, the American Museum of Natural History found a Diplodocus skeleton at Como Bluff.
facts.quote: The American Museum of Natural History was the first to launch an expedition, finding a semi-articulated partial postcranial skeleton containing many vertebrae of Diplodocus in at Como Bluff in 1897.

facts.statement: A massive Diplodocus skeleton was discovered in 1899 in Sheep Creek, Wyoming, on an expedition funded by Andrew Carnegie.
facts.quote: The most notable Diplodocus find also came in 1899 on an expedition funded by Scottish-American steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie, when crew members from the Carnegie Museum of Natural History discovered a massive and well preserved skeleton of Diplodocus in the Morrison Formation of Sheep Creek, Wyoming.

facts.statement: In 1900, Carnegie crews led by John Bell Hatcher, William Jacob Holland, and Charles Gilmore found another Diplodocus skeleton near the first one.
facts.quote: In 1900, Carnegie crews returned to Sheep Creek on an expedition led by John Bell Hatcher, William Jacob Holland, and Charles Gilmore and discovered another well preserved skeleton of Diplodocus adjacent to the specimen collected in 1899.

facts.statement: In 1909, Earl Douglass found Diplodocus fossils at Dinosaur National Monument in the Kimmeridgian Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: The Carnegie Museum of Natural History made another landmark discovery in 1909 when Earl Douglass unearthed several caudal vertebrae from Apatosaurus in what is now Dinosaur National Monument on the border region between Colorado and Utah, with the sandstone dating to the Kimmeridgian of the Morrison Formation.

facts.statement: Between 1909 and 1922, the Carnegie Museum excavated over 120 dinosaur individuals and more than 1,600 bones at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: From 1909 to 1922, with the Carnegie Museum excavating the quarry, eventually unearthing over 120 dinosaur individuals and 1,600+ bones, many of the associated skeletons being very complete and are on display in several American museums.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass found a semi-articulated diplodocine skull with mandibles in 1912 at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: In 1912, Douglass found a semi articulated skull of a diplodocine with mandibles (CM 11161) in the Monument.

facts.statement: Carnegie crews found skull CM 3452 in 1915 and skull CM 1155 in 1923 at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: Another skull (CM 3452) was found by Carnegie crews in 1915, bearing 6 articulated cervical vertebrae and mandibles, and another skull with mandibles (CM 1155) was found in 1923.

facts.statement: William Jacob Holland described the Dinosaur National Monument skulls in 1924 and referred them to Diplodocus longus.
facts.quote: All of the skulls found at Dinosaur National Monument were shipped back to Pittsburgh and described by William Jacob Holland in detail in 1924, who referred the specimens to D. longus.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass collected the first known juvenile Diplodocus skull in 1921.
facts.quote: A nearly complete skull of a juvenile Diplodocus was collected by Douglass in 1921, and it is the first known from a Diplodocus.

facts.statement: The National Museum of Natural History collected a Diplodocus skeleton at the Carnegie Quarry in 1923.
facts.quote: Another Diplodocus skeleton was collected at the Carnegie Quarry in Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, by the National Museum of Natural History in 1923.

facts.statement: The USNM V 10865 skeleton is one of the most complete Diplodocus specimens, featuring a well-preserved dorsal column.
facts.quote: The skeleton (USNM V 10865) is one of the most complete known from Diplodocus, consisting of a semi-articulated partial postcranial skeleton, including a well preserved dorsal column.

facts.statement: The Denver Museum of Nature and Science received a Diplodocus specimen from the Carnegie Museum that was collected at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: The Denver Museum of Nature and Science obtained a Diplodocus specimen through exchange from the Carnegie Museum that had been collected at Dinosaur National Monument.

facts.statement: Detailed analysis suggests the original type specimen of Diplodocus longus is dubious.
facts.quote: detailed analysis has discovered that this type specimen is actually dubious, which is not an ideal situation for the type species of a well-known genus like Diplodocus.

facts.statement: A proposal to change the type species of Diplodocus to D. carnegii was rejected by the ICZN because Hatcher failed to prove D. carnegii was distinct from D. longus.
facts.quote: A petition to the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature was being considered which proposed making D. carnegii the new type species. This proposal was rejected by the ICZN and D. longus has been maintained as the type species, because Hatcher did not demonstrate why the specimen he called Diplodocus carnegii was not actually just a more complete specimen of Diplodocus longus.

facts.statement: In 2015, Tschopp et al. classified the first complete diplodocid skull as an indeterminate diplodocine due to a lack of overlap with diagnostic Diplodocus postcranial material.
facts.quote: Tschopp et al.'s analysis placed it as an indeterminate diplodocine in 2015 due to the lack of overlap with any diagnostic Diplodocus postcranial material, as was the fate with all skulls assigned to Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Emmanuel Tschopp et al. determined that AMNH FR 223 belongs to D. hallorum, not D. longus.
facts.quote: In Emmanuel Tschopp et al.'s phylogenetic analysis of Diplodocidae, AMNH FR 223 was found to be not a skeleton of D. longus, but the later named species D. hallorum.

facts.statement: Suzannah Maidment (2024) suggests AMNH FR 223 is the geologically youngest specimen of D. hallorum based on its location in systems tract 6.
facts.quote: As seen in the supplementary work done by Suzannah Maidment (2024), AMNH FR 223 also appears to be the geologically youngest specimen of D. hallorum, as the quarry it was found in is within systems tract 6 (C6), which contains the youngest deposits in the Morrison Formation, as opposed to the other specimens of the taxon which were found in the older systems tract 4 (B4, which dates range from 151.88 Ma to 149.1 Ma).

facts.statement: Emmanuel Tschopp et al. classified the USNM V 10865 skeleton as belonging to D. hallorum.
facts.quote: In Emmanuel Tschopp et al.'s phylogenetic analysis of Diplodocidae, USNM V 10865 was also found to be an individual of D. hallorum.

facts.statement: In 1979, hikers discovered Diplodocus vertebrae near San Ysidro, New Mexico.
facts.quote: Few Diplodocus finds came for many years until 1979, when three hikers came across several vertebrae stuck in elevated stone next to several petroglyphs in a canyon west of San Ysidro, New Mexico.

facts.statement: An expedition led by David D. Gillette collected a Diplodocus specimen between 1985 and 1990.
facts.quote: The find was reported to the New Mexican Museum of Natural History, who dispatched an expedition led by David D. Gillette in 1985, that collected the specimen after several visits from 1985 to 1990.

facts.statement: Specimen NMMNH P-3690 was found in semi-articulation with 230 gastroliths and deposited at the New Mexican Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: The specimen was preserved in semi-articulation, including 230 gastroliths, with several vertebrae, partial pelvis, and right femur and was prepared and deposited at the New Mexican Museum of Natural History under NMMNH P-3690.

facts.statement: David D. Gillette named the specimen Seismosaurus halli in 1991.
facts.quote: The specimen was not described until 1991 in the Journal of Paleontology, where Gillette named it Seismosaurus halli

facts.statement: In 1994, the name was amended to Seismosaurus hallorum.
facts.quote: In 1994, Gillette published an amendment changing the name to S. hallorum.

facts.statement: Seismosaurus was synonymized with Diplodocus in 2004 and 2006.
facts.quote: In 2004 and later 2006, Seismosaurus was synonymized with Diplodocus

facts.statement: The Museum of the Rockies discovered the Mother's Day Quarry in Montana in 1994.
facts.quote: In 1994, the Museum of the Rockies discovered a very productive fossil site at Mother's Day Quarry in Carbon County, Montana from the Salt Wash member of the Morrison Formation

facts.statement: The Mother's Day Quarry yielded isolated Diplodocus bones ranging from juveniles to adults in pristine condition.
facts.quote: The quarry was very productive, having mostly isolated Diplodocus bones from juveniles to adults in pristine preservation.

facts.statement: The quarry contained a disparity in age groups and frequent preservation of skin impressions, pathologies, and articulated specimens.
facts.quote: The quarry notably had a great disparity between the amount of juveniles and adults in the quarry, as well as the frequent preservation of skin impressions, pathologies, and some articulated specimens from Diplodocus.

facts.statement: A nearly complete juvenile skull found at the quarry highlights ontogenetic dietary changes in Diplodocus.
facts.quote: One specimen, a nearly complete skull of a juvenile Diplodocus, was found at the quarry and is one of few known and highlighted ontogenetic dietary changes in the genus.

facts.statement: Diagnostic Diplodocus remains were found in Spain in 2026 but were not assigned to a specific species.
facts.quote: In 2026, diagnostic remains of Diplodocus were found in the Upper Jurassic Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Spain, but not assigned to any particular species.

facts.statement: Diplodocus is the type genus and namesake of the family Diplodocidae.
facts.quote: Diplodocus is both the type genus of, and gives its name to, the Diplodocidae, the family in which it belongs.

facts.statement: Diplodocids are characterized by long necks and tails, a horizontal posture, and forelimbs shorter than hind limbs.
facts.quote: All are characterized by long necks and tails and a horizontal posture, with forelimbs shorter than hind limbs.

facts.statement: The subfamily Diplodocinae includes Diplodocus and its closest relatives, such as Barosaurus.
facts.quote: A subfamily, the Diplodocinae, was erected to include Diplodocus and its closest relatives, including Barosaurus.

facts.statement: Apatosaurus is considered a diplodocid but belongs to the sister subfamily Apatosaurinae, not Diplodocinae.
facts.quote: More distantly related is the contemporaneous Apatosaurus, which is still considered a diplodocid, although not a diplodocine, as it is a member of the sister subfamily Apatosaurinae.

facts.statement: Some authors identify Dinheirosaurus and Tornieria as close relatives of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The Portuguese Dinheirosaurus and the African Tornieria have also been identified as close relatives of Diplodocus by some authors.

facts.statement: The clade Diplodocoidea includes diplodocids, dicraeosaurids, rebbachisaurids, Suuwassea, Amphicoelias, possibly Haplocanthosaurus, and/or nemegtosaurids.
facts.quote: Diplodocoidea comprises the diplodocids, as well as the dicraeosaurids, rebbachisaurids, Suuwassea, Amphicoelias possibly Haplocanthosaurus, and/or the nemegtosaurids.

facts.statement: Diplodocoidea is the sister group to Macronaria, which includes camarasaurids, brachiosaurids, and titanosaurians.
facts.quote: The clade is the sister group to Macronaria (camarasaurids, brachiosaurids and titanosaurians).

facts.statement: Diplodocus carnegii, named after Andrew Carnegie, was described and named by John Bell Hatcher in 1901.
facts.quote: Diplodocus carnegii (also spelled incorrectly D. carnegiei), named after Andrew Carnegie, is the best known, mainly due to a near-complete skeleton known as Dippy (specimen CM 84) collected by Jacob Wortman, of the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and described and named by John Bell Hatcher in 1901.

facts.statement: Diplodocus hallorum was first described in 1991 as Seismosaurus halli from specimen NMMNH P-3690.
facts.quote: Diplodocus hallorum, first described in 1991 by Gillette as Seismosaurus halli from a partial skeleton comprising vertebrae, pelvis and ribs (specimen NMMNH P-3690).

facts.statement: The specific name hallorum honors Jim and Ruth Hall, and the emended name was followed by researchers including Carpenter in 2006.
facts.quote: As the specific name honors two people, Jim and Ruth Hall (of Ghost Ranch), George Olshevsky later suggested to emend the name as S. hallorum, using the mandatory genitive plural; Gillette then emended the name, which usage has been followed by others, including Carpenter (2006).

facts.statement: In 2004, a presentation argued that Seismosaurus was a junior synonym of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: In 2004, a presentation at the annual conference of the Geological Society of America made a case for Seismosaurus being a junior synonym of Diplodocus.

facts.statement: A 2006 publication renamed the species Diplodocus hallorum and speculated it might be the same as D. longus.
facts.quote: This was followed by a much more detailed publication in 2006, which not only renamed the species Diplodocus hallorum, but also speculated that it could prove to be the same as D. longus.

facts.statement: A 2015 analysis noted that opinions on D. hallorum were based on more complete referred specimens of D. longus.
facts.quote: A 2015 analysis of diplodocid relationships noted that these opinions are based on the more complete referred specimens of Diplodocus longus.

facts.statement: Detailed analysis suggests the original fossil of D. longus lacks necessary features for comparison with other specimens.
facts.quote: Though several more complete specimens have been attributed to D. longus, detailed analysis has suggested that the original fossil lacks the necessary features to allow comparison with other specimens.

facts.statement: Diplodocus lacustris was named by Marsh in 1884 based on a snout with slender teeth from Morrison, Colorado.
facts.quote: Diplodocus lacustris was named by Marsh in 1884 based on a snout with comparatively slender teeth (YPM 1922) from Morrison, Colorado.

facts.statement: In 2015, Tschopp and colleagues argued that the snout belonged to Camarasaurus and the teeth could not be identified to a particular genus.
facts.quote: In 2015, Tschopp and colleagues argued that the snout of the specimen actually belonged to Camarasaurus, and that the teeth cannot be identified to a particular genus.

facts.statement: D. lacustris is considered an indeterminate diplodocid and a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: D. lacustris would therefore be an indeterminate diplodocid and a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Diplodocus hayi was named by William Jacob Holland in 1924 based on a braincase and partial skeleton found near Sheridan, Wyoming.
facts.quote: Diplodocus hayi was named by William Jacob Holland in 1924 based on a braincase and partial postcranial skeleton (HMNS 175), including a nearly complete vertebral column, found in the Morrison Formation strata near Sheridan, Wyoming.

facts.statement: In 2015, Tschopp and colleagues reassessed D. hayi as its own genus, Galeamopus.
facts.quote: D. hayi remained a species of Diplodocus until reassessment by Emmanuel Tschopp and colleagues determined that it was its own genus, Galeamopus, in 2015.

facts.statement: The reassessment found that skulls AMNH 969 and USNM 2673 referred to Galeamopus, not Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The reassessment also found that the skulls AMNH 969 and USNM 2673 were not Diplodocus either and actually referred specimens of Galeamopus.

facts.statement: Marsh and Hatcher assumed Diplodocus was aquatic due to the position of its nasal openings.
facts.quote: Marsh and then Hatcher assumed that the animal was aquatic, because of the position of its nasal openings at the apex of the cranium.

facts.statement: A 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates sauropods likely could not breathe through nostrils when submerged due to water pressure.
facts.quote: A 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates that sauropods probably could not have breathed through their nostrils when the rest of the body was submerged, as the water pressure on the chest wall would be too great.

facts.statement: Reconstructions show Diplodocus had great pneumaticity in the neck and thorax, which could have aided respiration.
facts.quote: Reconstructions of the neck and thorax of Diplodocus show great pneumaticity, which could have played a role in respiration as it does in birds.

facts.statement: A 1910 reconstruction by Oliver P. Hay depicted Diplodocus with splayed, lizard-like limbs.
facts.quote: a classic 1910 reconstruction by Oliver P. Hay depicts two Diplodocus with splayed lizard-like limbs on the banks of a river.

facts.statement: Sauropod footprints found in the 1930s refuted the hypothesis that Diplodocus had a sprawling, lizard-like gait.
facts.quote: Finds of sauropod footprints in the 1930s eventually put Hay's theory to rest.

facts.statement: Studies on sauropod neck morphology suggest the neutral posture of Diplodocus was horizontal rather than vertical.
facts.quote: Studies looking at the morphology of sauropod necks have concluded that the neutral posture of Diplodocus neck was close to horizontal, rather than vertical

facts.statement: The alignment of the inner ear in diplodocoids contradicts the hypothesis that Diplodocus held its neck at a highly elevated angle.
facts.quote: However, this idea might be contradicted due to the inner ear of diplodocoids actually being in alignment for a horizontal neck pose.

facts.statement: A 1992 study suggested that the longest-necked diplodocids required a heart weighing 1.6 tons, roughly a tenth of their body weight.
facts.quote: A 1992 Columbia University study of diplodocid neck structure indicated that the longest necks would have required a 1.6-ton heart

facts.statement: Some researchers argue that a near-horizontal head and neck posture eliminated the need for auxiliary hearts by keeping the brain at a manageable height.
facts.quote: Some argue that the near-horizontal posture of the head and neck would have eliminated the problem of supplying blood to the brain, as it would not be elevated.

facts.statement: The genus Diplodocus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1878

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Diplodocus is Diplodocus carnegii.
facts.quote: type_species: Diplodocus carnegii

facts.statement: Seismosaurus is listed as a synonym of Diplodocus, a classification proposed by Gillette in 1991.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Seismosaurus Gillette, 1991

facts.statement: Diplodocus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage, between 154 and 152 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivieron a finales del período Jurásico Superior, entre 154 a 152 millones de años, durante el Kimmeridgiense

facts.statement: Diplodocus fossils have been found in what is now North America and Teruel, Spain.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy son Norteamérica y Teruel (Aragón, España)

facts.statement: Diplodocus was one of the most common dinosaurs in the upper layers of the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: El Diplodocus es uno de los dinosaurios más comunes de la parte superior de la Formación Morrison

facts.statement: Diplodocus is easily identifiable by its classic form, long neck and tail, and four robust legs.
facts.quote: El Diplodocus está entre los dinosaurios más fácilmente identificables, con su forma clásica, cuello y cola largos, y cuatro patas robustas.

facts.statement: Diplodocus is among the best-known dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Los Diplodocus están entre los dinosaurios mejor conocidos.

facts.statement: Diplodocus were very large quadrupeds with long necks and extensive tails shaped like whips.
facts.quote: Fueron animales cuadrúpedos muy grandes, de cuello largo y con una extensa cola en forma de látigo.

facts.statement: Diplodocus had front limbs slightly shorter than their hind limbs, resulting in a predominantly horizontal posture.
facts.quote: Sus miembros delanteros eran ligeramente más cortos que los traseros, lo que configura una postura predominantemente horizontal.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Diplodocus carnegii (CM 84) is estimated to be about 25 meters long and 6.5 meters high at the neck.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo de Diplodocus carnegii, CM 84 es el más completo hallado de su género, estimado en alrededor de 25 metros de largo y 6.5 m de alto al cuello.

facts.statement: Mass estimates for Diplodocus carnegii range from 11.5 to 19.7 metric tons.
facts.quote: Las estimaciones de su masa se sitúan en el rango de 11,5 a 19,7 toneladas

facts.statement: Recent revisions show that the giant tail vertebrae used to estimate D. hallorum's size were actually located further back in the tail than originally thought.
facts.quote: Una revisión más reciente demuestra que las vértebras gigantes de la cola estaban colocadas realmente más adelante en la cola que lo que D. Gillete las había ubicado originalmente.

facts.statement: The skeleton of Diplodocus hallorum at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History included a thirteenth tail vertebra belonging to another animal, which reduced the estimated size of D. hallorum.
facts.quote: El estudio demuestra que el esqueleto completo del Diplodocus en el Museo Carnegie de Historia Natural de Pittsburgh, Pensilvania, en el cual las estimaciones de Diplodocus (Seismosaurus) hallorum se basaron, incluía la decimotercera vértebra de la cola perteneciente a otro animal

facts.statement: After correction, the estimated length of Diplodocus hallorum is approximately 32 meters and its weight is between 25 and 30 metric tons.
facts.quote: quedando en aproximadamente 32 metros de largo y 25-30 toneladas.

facts.statement: The name Diplodocus is derived from Greek words meaning 'double' and 'beam', referring to the chevron-shaped bones along the lower tail.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico Diplodocus es la forma en neolatín derivada del griego διπλόος (diploös) «doble» y δοκός (dokos) «viga», en referencia a la forma de los huesos en chevrón a lo largo de la parte inferior de la cola.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh coined the term Diplodocus in 1878, believing the chevron-shaped tail bones were exclusive to the genus.
facts.quote: El término fue cuñado por Othniel Charles Marsh en 1878, pensando que esta forma de los huesos en chevróne era exclusiva de los Diplodocus.

facts.statement: The large size of Diplodocus may have deterred predators like Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus, which coexisted with it in the same geological layers.
facts.quote: Su gran tamaño pudo haber sido un impedimento para los depredadores Allosaurus y Ceratosaurus, cuyos restos se han encontrado en los mismos estratos, lo que sugiere que coexistieron con el Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Diplodocus had a neck formed by at least 15 vertebrae.
facts.quote: Su cuello estaba formado por al menos 15 vértebras

facts.statement: Researchers believe Diplodocus could not raise its neck more than 30 degrees above its horizontal axis.
facts.quote: no más de 30 grados por encima de su eje horizontal

facts.statement: No skull has ever been found that can be said with certainty to belong to Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Nunca se ha encontrado un cráneo del que se pueda decir con certeza que pertenece al Diplodocus

facts.statement: Diplodocus had small, forward-pointing peg-shaped teeth located only in the front sections of its jaws.
facts.quote: Diplodocus tenía pequeños dientes en forma de "clavija" que apuntaban hacia adelante

facts.statement: It is debated whether Diplodocus had a trunk; recent studies claim there is no paleoneuroanatomical evidence to support the hypothesis of a trunk.
facts.quote: Ha habido especulaciones acerca de si tal configuración significa que los Diplodocus tuvieron una trompa. Pero un estudio reciente afirmó que no hay evidencias paleoneuroanatómicas que respalden la hipótesis de la trompa

facts.statement: Diplodocus had an extremely long tail composed of more than 80 caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Los Diplodocus tenían una cola extremadamente larga, compuesta de más de 80 vértebras caudales

facts.statement: The middle part of the Diplodocus tail had strange chevron-shaped bones called 'double beams'.
facts.quote: La parte media de la cola tenía "dobles vigas", huesos cheurones de forma extraña

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that Diplodocus may have used its tail for defense or to make noise like a whip.
facts.quote: Existen especulaciones acerca de que los diplódocos podrían haber utilizado su cola como defensa o para hacer ruido como un látigo

facts.statement: The tail may have served as a counterweight for the neck.
facts.quote: También podría haber servido como contrapeso para el cuello

facts.statement: Diplodocus lacked claws except for the first finger of the hand.
facts.quote: El Diplodocus carecía de garras a excepción del dedo 1 de la mano

facts.statement: The function of the unusually specialized claw on the first finger is unknown.
facts.quote: La función de esta garra inusualmente especializada es desconocida

facts.statement: Recent discoveries suggest Diplodocus and other diplodocids may have had narrow, pointed keratin spines around the back.
facts.quote: Recientes descubrimientos han demostrado que los Diplodocus y otros diplodócidos pudieron haber tenido unas estrechas y puntiagudas espinas de queratina alrededor del dorso

facts.statement: These spines could have been up to 18 centimeters high on the tail.
facts.quote: de hasta 18 centímetros de alto en su cola

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Diplodocus is Diplodocus longus.
facts.quote: Type species: Diplodocus longus

facts.statement: The parent group of Diplodocus is Diplodocinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Diplodocinae

facts.statement: Diplodocus belongs to the family Diplodocidae.
facts.quote: Family: Diplodocidae

facts.statement: Diplodocus is classified in the class Saurischia.
